ops.old: For a lower-impact cruise, fewer vessels in the same area means less collective pressure on the bay and a calmer experience for each guest. Green Ruby sails both bays with two identical ships: Green Ruby 1 on Ha Long Bay and Green Ruby 2 on Lan Ha Bay.
ops.new: Fewer boats make for a calmer experience, but a quieter bay is not in itself proof of a lower environmental impact: what each ship has on board, how it treats its wastewater and how it is operated matter more. Green Ruby will sail both bays with two identical ships, with first departures planned for February 2027: Green Ruby 1 on Ha Long Bay and Green Ruby 2 on Lan Ha Bay.
ops.note: EN #221 fewer boats != lower impact (decision 4); present tense "sails" -> will sail, Feb 2027 (not yet in service)

ops.old: From 27 September 2026, EU rules (the Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive) ban generic environmental claims and sustainability labels that are not backed by evidence or certification when marketing to European consumers. For operators selling to European travellers, substantiated claims are a legal requirement, not only a brand choice.
ops.new: EU consumer law offers a useful reference here. Since 27 September 2026, rules introduced by Directive (EU) 2024/825, the Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive, set out how environmental claims made to European consumers are judged: generic claims such as "eco-friendly" or "green" that are not backed by recognised evidence, and sustainability labels that are not based on a certification scheme or set up by public authorities, are no longer allowed. Whatever rules apply to a given operator, the same test works for any traveller: is the claim specific, and can it be checked?
ops.note: EN #221 EU Directive 2024/825 presented only as a reference for how claims are judged for EU consumers, not as an obligation on operators/Green Ruby

ops.old: Is Green Globe certification recognised internationally? Yes. Green Globe is accredited by the Global Sustainable Tourism Council (GSTC), which sets international criteria for credible tourism certification, and it is widely recognised in the luxury travel trade.
ops.new: What is Green Globe certification? Green Globe is a certification programme for travel and tourism businesses. Its standard sets 44 core criteria across sustainable management, social and economic impact, cultural heritage and the environment, and members are assessed through independent audits, including on-site audits. ops.old: Depuis le 27 septembre 2026, la réglementation européenne (la directive sur la responsabilisation des consommateurs pour la transition verte) interdit, dans la communication destinée aux consommateurs européens, les allégations environnementales génériques et les labels de durabilité qui ne reposent ni sur des preuves ni sur une certification. Pour les opérateurs qui s’adressent aux voyageurs européens, étayer ses affirmations est donc une obligation légale, et plus seulement un choix d’image.
ops.new: Le droit européen de la consommation offre ici un repère utile. Depuis le 27 septembre 2026, les règles issues de la directive (UE) 2024/825, dite directive sur la responsabilisation des consommateurs pour la transition verte, précisent comment sont appréciées les allégations environnementales adressées aux consommateurs européens : les allégations génériques comme « écologique » ou « vert » qui ne s’appuient pas sur des preuves reconnues, et les labels de durabilité qui ne reposent ni sur un système de certification ni sur une initiative des pouvoirs publics, n’y sont plus admis. Quelles que soient les règles applicables à tel ou tel opérateur, le critère vaut pour tout voyageur : l’affirmation est-elle précise, et peut-on la vérifier ?
ops.note: FR #289 EU Directive 2024/825 as a reference only, not an obligation on operators/Green Ruby
